title: Cap a real bee cell from inside an OpenCode session
action: E4's proof, the one D4/D5 rest on: a bee worker must actually run and cap a cell from inside an OpenCode session, not merely be defined. Create a throwaway proof cell through the CLI (bee cells add — a trivial, real change such as a one-line docs touch under docs/history/opencode-support/, with its own id, never one of this feature's cells), then run an `opencode run` session that dispatches the bee-build worker agent against it and let that session's worker do the whole loop: read the cell, make the change, commit, and cap through `bee cells finish`. Record in discovery.md: the exact invocation, whether dispatch went through the task tool or an @-mention, which model each tier actually resolved to, whether the guard plugin engaged inside the sub-session (a nested dispatch is where a belt most often goes missing), and the wall-clock shape of sequential dispatch (D5). If the free provider cannot carry a worker-sized prompt, that is a named blocker with its evidence — never a simulated or hand-run substitute presented as the proof.

truths: A cell was capped by a worker running inside an OpenCode session — transcript excerpt recorded
The guard plugin's engagement inside the sub-session is a recorded fact, either way
Model resolution per tier is recorded from the session, not from config
A failure to run is a named blocker with evidence, never a substituted proof

trace.outcome: proved E4 live: a bee-build subagent capped a real cell (lv-1) from inside a nested OpenCode task-tool dispatch, after naming two real gaps (reservation session-id mismatch on nested dispatch; --agent flag not reaching subagents)
